title: Develop
description: A wooden utility pole shot from its foot, straight up through its crossarms and cables into summer cumulus, coming up like a print in a darkroom tray, except that the developer runs through the scene's depth rather than across the paper. It opens as a print does, the darkest, nearest wood first, at the foot of the pole, and climbs it. Drag and it climbs the pole over the first half of the drag, the sky waiting behind it latent and out of focus, then comes up through the crossarms and out along the spans, and only then does a soft, wide band of warm light carry on through the cloud's depth, racking the sky into focus; start from a blank sheet on the sky and it runs the other way, from the far sky towards you. Behind it the photograph has arrived, sharp and in full colour. Ahead of it the scene is not there yet: the sky a faint, light latent print in its own blue, out of focus by as much as the depth still to cover, the cloud melting rather than breaking into bokeh, and the pole and its cables not there at all, a latent image being invisible, so they come up out of the sky at the front, always sharp, the frame's one crisp anchor: the structure develops along its own length, up the pole and out through its knot of crossarms, and past the knot each span comes up whole, out to the frame's edge, so no wire ever stops short in mid-air. In the sky the depth is the cloud's own, so the cores come up first and the front threads the cumulus. Let go and the front carries your speed, then the print settles. Drag back to undo it.
intent: One depth-keyed reveal from herb's CrowdVolt depth research (factory/reality/crowdvolt-depth-heroes.md: a front sweeps a key 0..1 through depth; scan, focus pull, assemble, strata), finished as a title sequence with the quality of a print coming up in a darkroom tray, in the summer-film genre (factory/reality/genre-spec.md). References: Saul Bass's and Pablo Ferro's title sequences that reveal an image by a moving edge (https://www.artofthetitle.com/), and the darkroom print emerging in developer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photographic_developer).

sources.author: Dina Lydia (@dinazina)
sources.note: 3593x2736, Seattle, a worm's-eye frame from the foot of the pole: its sides converge on a vanishing point in the upper third of the frame, the cables and braces radiate out of it, cumulus all round. Cropped to a full-width 3:2 band (rows 200-2595) and shipped at 2400x1600. Re-plated from the earlier PJH (@dokae) catenary mast in Ine (unsplash 6DHLBwmRkOw), a 40-degree look up that read as an ordinary snapshot. Depth Anything V2 Small (tools/depth/depth_hr.py), prepared as in herb's notes (percentile normalise, median, dilate near values, slight blur). Split into two layers: the sky with the pole, crossarms, braces and every cable painted out (LaMa, big-lama ONNX, at half size through a mask dilated well past the silhouettes, matched to the sky round each hole in log light, grain put back; shown only a few pixels past the structure, the photo's own sky beyond), and the structure as a known-background matte over it (alpha = (I-B).(F-B)/|F-B|^2; cables found by a black-hat on luma; the bright hardware, lit braces and insulators, found as narrow features lighter or darker than the local sky that hang off the structure, and matted against the painted sky; the matte is pulled against a log-light normalised-convolution fill). The structure develops not by its depth (the depth model sees a two-pixel cable only in patches, so the wires came up as tapered slivers and floating fragments) but by its reach: the geodesic distance from the pole's foot measured inside the matte, monotonic outward along every cable and brace and the same across a cable's width (bake.py --reach, reach.png, 16 bit); past the knot (the matte's density round the crossarms, with the pole's wood whole) the spans fall into a few webs of crossing cables, each brought up whole, on the plate's own wire, once the last cable leading into it has grown out to it (span_of, reach.png B). The sky key's distance term is measured from the zenith the pole points at, and the sky is graded round it in the bake, in log light: deep cobalt overhead opening to a paler cyan at the corners, the cloud's rims turned off lilac to a cyan-grey and its tops warmed to a neutral. Bake: tools/depth/bakes/develop/bake.py. The structure is all that is kept of this photograph: its own sky (a pale cerulean with small, flat-white curds) was replaced (bake.py --sky, SKY_PLATES) by two photographs of congestus towers against a deep summer sky, CC0 (next sources), laid as plates: each put in by a homography, never resampled along curves, turned so its towers lean in on the pole's vanishing point with a gentle keystone (LEAN 0.35) that converges its verticals on it, and taken down to the print's scale by area first, so every cauliflower curd keeps the photograph's own detail and comes up fully sharp once developed. The big tower on the right reaches in almost to the zenith and the one on the left stands lower and further out, so the open cobalt overhead is an uneven gap between two towers, not a ring round a disc. (It replaces a stereographic re-wind of two horizon photographs round the zenith, which smeared the towers radially and stood them in a ring round a stencilled hole of cobalt.) The plates are laid one over another by their cloud only: each one's clear sky, pushed in under its cloud from the open blue, is graded to the print's (cobalt round the zenith opening to cyan) by a per-channel gain, and the cloud takes only its light's share of that gain, so it keeps its own colour; the cloud's share is how far a pixel has gone from that sky's saturated blue towards a neutral, or a stop or more under it (a slate base in deep shade). The structure is laid over it through the same matte, taken out of the photograph against its own sky round it (F = (I - (1 - alpha) x B) / alpha, held inside the colour range of the opaque steel round it, so no pale cerulean rides on the cobalt), the matte floored and choked by about a pixel, thin wires matted again as dark steel, and the sky caught between the crossarm members dropped. The cloud is laid as photographed right out to its edge, and its light, with its fine modelling steepened a little, is set on a ramp in log light from the skylight to the sun: the sunlit tops a warm white at 0.93, under paper white, which the print's shoulder carries on to a glow without clipping; the shaded undersides and folds the clear sky round them, greyed a little and lifted a touch inside a tower, a soft skylight blue rather than a slate; and at the cloud's edge the ramp's foot is the local sky itself, so the photograph's slate base and the grey mix of base and sky along each underside go to the blue round it and the base fades into the sky instead of ending on a dark tide line (its light pushed out over the edge from just inside, the previous fix, laid a pale band along every base with the slate showing just past it); the sky key measured again from the new cloud.
